Name: Gretchen Haer
Badge: Teacher as Researcher: Cultivating Literacy Routines
Looking back on this inquiry cycle, what did you learn about your teaching and your students that you might not have noticed otherwise? How did engaging in this teacher-research process shape or shift your thinking about your classroom practice?:

Engaging in this teacher-research process shifted my thinking through helping me realize its okay to try things. I constantly get in the headspace if I don't have every detail planned and their is a potential to 'waste time' I should attempt it in my class. However by DOING and having semi-deadlines to try these practices gave me the extra push to do it when I didn't feel fully prepared. The result? Student engagement and way more effective formative assessments. So you could say it taught me to go ahead and do, because even doing it feeling underprepared, I had higher engagement then the other way.

Share one artifact or anecdote from trying out your chosen strategy (e.g., a piece of student work, notes from your Writer’s Notebook, a classroom snapshot, or a brief story from the experience).:
What new questions or next steps are you leaving this module with? How might you continue to explore or build on this inquiry in your future teaching?:

Next steps is to implement these strategies consistently. They say I say is easy to do with my resources and annotations but I want to get better at reminding my students to USE their writer's notebooks. I need to deliberately put in my lesson plans the strategies I plan on using that day. My goal was 3 a week.
